extracted.intended_audience: researchers, journal editors, research-integrity sleuths, science journalists, and readers interested in academic misconduct and retractions
extracted.subtask_description: A news roundup page reporting recent cases, studies, and developments relating to research integrity, retractions, and scientific misconduct. It summarizes incidents (retractions, debarments, court rulings), analyses of trends (fabricated references), and resources for tracking retractions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fabricated data / intentional fabrication
rubrics_metrics.description: Intentional fabrication of data across papers, manuscripts, presentations and grant applications (e.g., 'Chemist Ariel Fernández intentionally fabricated data in 12 grant-supported papers, four unpublished manuscripts, one presentation and three grant applications').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Findings of intentional fabrication can lead to retraction of publications and administrative sanctions such as funding debarment (example: ORI announced a 15-year funding debarment). Related procedural notes: ORI posts notices and actions may be published in the Federal Register; administrative law judge (ALJ) decisions and appeals are part of the process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plagiarism / pattern_of_plagiarism
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'pattern of plagiarism' in books or other works (extensive copying across texts) is treated as scientific misconduct and can trigger repayment orders and funding bans.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequences include orders to repay grant funding, multi-year bans from applying for funding (example: five-year ban), and reputational/legal consequences; courts may review foundation findings and procedural complaints by the accused.

rubrics_metrics.name: Image manipulation / AI-altered imagery
rubrics_metrics.description: Altering images (including using AI) in research outputs — e.g., clinical imagery manipulated with AI or superimposed elements — constitutes grounds for retraction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journals may retract items when authors acknowledge manipulated imagery (example: NEJM retracted an image after authors admitted using AI to superimpose a tape ruler). Editors and readers should scrutinize striking photographic evidence; admission of manipulation typically triggers retraction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fabricated references / hallucinated citations
rubrics_metrics.description: References cited in papers that do not exist or were generated (e.g., AI-hallucinated citations). The page reports an analysis finding 'one in 277 PubMed-indexed papers in 2026 referenced a paper that didn’t exist.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detection can use AI tools to 'distinguish genuine fabrications from formatting discrepancies such as informally abbreviated titles.' A sharp increase in hallucinated references coincided with the rise of AI writing tools; such findings can prompt corrections/retractions and broader concern about AI-generated content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Citation manipulation / citation_stuffing
rubrics_metrics.description: Patterns of citation stuffing or citation manipulation (excessive/self-serving citations favoring a particular author) in conference proceedings or journals are indicators of unethical behavior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sleuthing and audits (e.g., blog posts summarizing problems) can reveal citation-stuffing patterns; such findings may result in public scrutiny and legal disputes (example: a sleuth was sued for defamation over posts accusing an author of citation stuffing, and a Swiss appeals court later overturned a defamation conviction).

rubrics_metrics.name: Data/image duplication / repeating_patterns
rubrics_metrics.description: Repeating patterns in data or identical images appearing across different papers (e.g., repeating patterns in electron microscopy data, identical cell images across papers) are red flags for data manipulation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publishers may retract papers when image/data duplication is confirmed (example: Journal of Materials Chemistry B retracted a paper after finding repeating image patterns and identical images used elsewhere). Comparison of images/graphs can reveal near-identical elements despite color/thickness changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorship misconduct / cheating in student competitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Allegations of cheating or plagiarizing in student science fair projects, especially when work appears implausibly advanced or overlaps with published research.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Competition rules (example: Vietnam Science and Engineering Fair/ViSEF rule that a project 'had to have been completed in 12 months') set eligibility standards; sleuths compare posters/graphs to published papers to spot overlaps. Violations can lead to controversy, investigations, and possible disqualification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lack of transparency in grant applications
rubrics_metrics.description: Lack of transparency during the grant application process is treated as aggravating conduct and may support findings of misconduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Foundations and courts may consider lack of transparency alongside plagiarism or fabrication when ordering repayment of funds or imposing bans, as in cases summarized in administrative decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural standards and consequences (ORI and administrative process)
rubrics_metrics.description: Research-misconduct adjudication follows administrative processes (investigations, ALJ decisions, appeals, Federal Register notices) and can result in sanctions such as debarment from federal funding for set periods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example workflow: an ORI finding may be recommended by an ALJ, posted by ORI, and published in the Federal Register; sanctions (e.g., 15-year debarment) take effect on a specified date and are recorded in exclusion records. Appeals and later reporting can clarify timelines and enforcement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of tracking resources as integrity indicators (databases/checkers)
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintaining and consulting curated lists/databases (e.g., Retraction Watch Database, Hijacked Journal Checker, lists of COVID-19 retractions, mass resignations list) is a standard practice for monitoring publication integrity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These resources provide counts and entries that indicate the scale of problems (example counts cited: over 64,000 retractions; Hijacked Journal Checker >400 entries; COVID-19 retractions ~650). The site encourages reliance on and support for these tools to track trends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal outcomes and standards in defamation / litigation over allegations
rubrics_metrics.description: Litigation related to allegations (defamation suits, court orders) interacts with research-integrity reporting; courts assess whether allegations are defamatory or justified by truth/evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a Swiss appeals court overturned a 2025 defamation conviction of a sleuth who identified citation manipulation, and ordered the plaintiff to pay legal costs. Legal rulings can clear or affirm sleuthing activities and affect public reporting practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detection and measurement of AI influence in research outputs and data collection
rubrics_metrics.description: Assessing the extent to which AI tools have influenced publications or survey responses (e.g., AI chatbots completing surveys; AI generating invalid references) is an emerging evaluation dimension.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Studies use detection tools (example: a Prolific-created detector found <1% likely chatbot responses across several companies, but higher rates in one company) and preprints/letters to journals document trends. Distinguishing human vs. AI-generated content requires specific analytic approaches and has implications for data quality and integrity.
